resources.string: That's right.
Single Phase Bug
The compiler does everything in one go.
They're phases in sequence. The output of one is the input of the next.
Lexical analysis hands tokens to syntax analysis.
A type error is caught in the lexical phase.
Types are the semantic phase's job.
Optimization comes before syntax analysis.
You can only optimize after understanding the code.
Swapped Error Bug
Every error is a syntax error.
Each phase catches one kind of error.
An undeclared variable is a semantic error.
A missing semicolon is a syntax error.
A stray @ in the code is a semantic error.
The scanner catches it: no token starts with @.
Twin Lexeme Bug
Token and lexeme are the same thing.
The lexeme is the text. The token carries the class (id, num, if) and the lexeme.
In total = 10, total is the lexeme and id is the token.
Two different lexemes can have the same token.
Each lexeme has a token all its own.
x and y have the same token: id.
Short Cut Bug
>= is two tokens: > and =.
The scanner takes the biggest piece that matches.
ifa is an identifier.
In x>=10, the scanner closes > as soon as it sees it.
It tries to stretch and closes >=.
ifa becomes the token if followed by a.
Longest match: ifa stays whole.
Common Word Bug
if is a name like any other.
When the length ties, the rule that comes first wins. The reserved word must come first.
In Flex, the rule that comes first wins the tie.
Longest match decides before rule order.
yytext holds the token's class.
yytext holds the lexeme.
Full Star Bug
a* requires at least one a.
The star accepts zero or more. The empty string is in.
a+ requires at least one a.
The empty string matches a*.
(ab)* accepts aba.
Only whole repetitions of ab.
Counting Regex Bug
A regex checks balanced parentheses.
A finite automaton can't count without a limit. That's what grammars are for.
a^n b^n is not a regular language.
A context-free grammar checks parentheses.
A DFA has infinite memory.
It only remembers the current state.
Forgotten Closure Bug
The DFA's start is just the NFA's start.
It's its closure: everything you reach without reading anything.
Each DFA state is a set of NFA states.
A set is final if it has a final NFA state.
After reading a letter, I don't need to close again.
Always close after the move.
Twins Bug
States with the same number of arrows are equal.
They're only twins if no string tells them apart.
A final state and a non-final one are never twins.
The table of pairs starts by splitting finals from non-finals.
The minimal automaton accepts another language.
The language is the same, with fewer states.
Swapped Terminal Bug
A terminal is what will still turn into something else.
A nonterminal is what gets replaced. A terminal stays until the end.
The leaves of a sentence's tree are terminals, or ε when a rule vanishes.
A sentence has only terminals.
A sentential form never has a nonterminal.
It can have both kinds of symbol.
Loose Else Bug
The else belongs to the outer if.
The else goes with the nearest if.
if a then if b then x else y has two trees in this grammar.
In practice, the else goes with the nearest if.
Rewriting the grammar never fixes the dangling else.
You can rewrite it by separating closed and open statements.
Two Sums Bug
Ambiguity is just a drawing detail.
Two trees give two results: 2 + 3 * 4 becomes 14 or 20.
An ambiguous grammar has a sentence with two trees.
Two different leftmost derivations of the same sentence prove ambiguity.
Every expression grammar is ambiguous.
With levels E, T and F it stops being ambiguous.
Endless Loop Bug
Left recursion only makes the parser slow.
It locks up the top-down parser: it calls the same rule without reading anything.
The bottom-up parser, which you see in the Fortress, accepts left recursion.
Right recursion locks up the top-down parser.
On the right, it reads a token before coming back.
Same Start Bug
Factoring changes the language.
The language is the same. It just puts off the choice.
Factoring adds a level to the tree.
Factoring fixes any LL(1) conflict.
Factoring only removes the common start. The dangling else, for example, still has two possible rules.
First Only Bug
FIRST is just the first symbol of the rule.
If it's a nonterminal, its FIRST counts. If it vanishes, look at the next one.
If B vanishes in A -> B C, the FIRST of C goes into the FIRST of A.
ε goes into the FIRST of A if A can become empty.
The FIRST of a terminal is empty.
The FIRST of a terminal is itself.
Empty FOLLOW Bug
ε can go into FOLLOW.
FOLLOW never has ε. It keeps what comes after, and the end is $.
$ goes into the FOLLOW of the start symbol.
The FOLLOW of A gets the FIRST of what comes after A, without ε.
If A closes B's rule, the FOLLOW of A goes into the FOLLOW of B.
It's the other way around: the FOLLOW of B goes into the FOLLOW of A.
Double Cell Bug
Two rules in the same cell is normal.
A cell with two rules is a conflict. The grammar is not LL(1).
The rule goes in the column of each symbol in the FIRST of its right side.
If the right side can vanish, the rule goes in the FOLLOW columns.
Every grammar without left recursion is LL(1).
Flipped Stack Bug
The right side goes on the stack in written order.
It goes in back to front, so the first symbol ends up on top.
A terminal on top must match the input.
An empty cell in the table means error.
The input ran out with the stack full: sentence accepted.
It only accepts with stack and input both at the dollar sign.
Early Token Bug
Every function reads a token before deciding.
The function looks at the current token and only moves on when it matches.
casaToken checks and moves the input forward.
Recursive descent runs E -> E + T as it is.
It would fall into infinite recursion.
Stop Everything Bug
At the first error, the compiler has to stop.
It recovers and keeps going, to show several errors.
Panic mode drops tokens until a sync token.
A semicolon is usually a good sync token.
Recovering from the error fixes the program.
It only lets it find the next errors.
Early Reduce Bug
Saw a right side on the stack? Reduce right away.
It depends on what comes next. With E + T on the stack and * in the input, shift.
Reducing swaps the top for the left side of the rule.
Shift-reduce does the rightmost derivation in reverse.
A handle is any piece equal to a right side.
The handle is the right piece to reduce now.
Short Closure Bug
Closure just copies the item.
If the dot is before a nonterminal, its rules come in.
The dot marks how far the rule was read.
An item with the dot at the end asks for a reduction.
Every LR(0) state has a single item.
The closure usually pulls in several.
Blind FOLLOW Bug
SLR reduces on any token.
Only on the tokens in the FOLLOW of the left side.
LR(0) reduces without looking at the input.
A shift-reduce conflict is a doubt between shifting and reducing.
If SLR has a conflict, the grammar is ambiguous.
Repeated State Bug
LALR has the states of LR(1).
LALR merges states with the same core. It ends up the size of SLR.
Merging states can create a reduce-reduce conflict.
Merging states doesn't create a new shift-reduce.
SLR and LALR use the same lookahead symbols.
SLR uses FOLLOW. LALR is more precise.
Swapped Precedence Bug
The first %left is the strongest.
With no declaration, on shift-reduce Bison shifts.
On reduce-reduce, Bison picks the last rule.
It picks the first one in the file.
Inherited Bug
Every attribute goes up the tree.
Synthesized goes up. Inherited goes down or comes from the side.
An S-attributed definition uses only synthesized attributes.
The type of an expression is usually synthesized.
An L-attributed definition can't have inherited attributes.
It can, coming from the parent or from the left.
Stretched Integer Bug
int + float is an error.
The compiler converts the int to float and goes on.
int + float results in float.
Coercion is an automatic conversion.
A float fits in an int without losing anything.
The part after the decimal point is lost.
Leaky Scope Bug
A variable inside the block is valid outside it.
Each block opens a scope. When it closes, its names vanish.
The lookup starts at the innermost scope.
Declaring x inside hides the x outside.
Using an undeclared variable is a lexical error.
It's a semantic error.
Fat Tree Bug
The AST is the whole parse tree.
The AST keeps only what matters. Parentheses and pass-through rules vanish.
( a + b ) has no parenthesis node in the AST.
The shape of the AST already shows the precedence.
The AST has more nodes than the parse tree.
It's leaner.
Long Sum Bug
A TAC line has several operations.
At most one operation per line. The rest goes to temporaries.
a + b * c becomes two lines.
t1 = b * c comes before t2 = a + t1.
A temporary is a variable the person declared.
The compiler creates it.
Lying Optimization Bug
Optimizing can change the result.
Optimization has to keep what the program does.
2 * 3 can become 6 at compile time.
Code that never runs can go.
x / x can always become 1.
With x equal to zero, the program raised an error.
Single Recursion Bug
A recursive function has just one record.
Each call pushes a new record.
The record holds parameters, locals and the return address.
On return, the record leaves the stack.
A local variable survives after the return.
It leaves together with the record.
Forgotten Load Bug
MIPS adds straight from memory.
MIPS only works on registers. First lw, then the math, then sw.
lw copies from memory to the register.
sw stores the register in memory.
add adds two memory addresses directly.
add only uses registers.
Infinite Register Bug
There's always a register for everyone.
There are few. Whatever doesn't fit goes to memory: that's a spill.
Temporaries alive at the same time interfere.
Coloring the graph means giving neighbors different registers.
Temporaries that don't interfere need different registers.
They can share the same one.
